analysis.one_liner: Requires federal contractors to pay workers a living wage instead of poverty pay.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 94 cosponsors but died in House committees without ever coming up for a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Any company holding a federal contract or subcontract over $10,000 would have to pay each worker on that contract at least $8.20 an hour, or whatever hourly wage lifts a full-time worker above the federal poverty line for a family of four — whichever is higher. Companies that cheated would face contract suspension, a five-year ban on new federal contracts, and would owe workers their unpaid wages plus an equal amount in damages. Small businesses and most modest-paying nonprofits would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers on federal contracts — janitors, food service workers, security guards, and others employed by companies paid with federal dollars — would get a guaranteed wage of at least $8.20 an hour or the poverty line for a family of four, whichever is greater. Workers shortchanged would be repaid unpaid wages plus an equal amount in liquidated damages, paid out by the Secretary of Labor from amounts recovered from employers [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Covers any employer on a federal contract or subcontract over $10,000, requiring pay of the greater of $8.20 an hour or the hourly wage needed to reach the federal poverty level for a family of four at 40 hours a week [S2][S3].
Bars employers from dodging the wage by firing workers and replacing them with trainees, apprentices, or other employees exempt from the requirement [S2][S3].

Enforces the wage with contract suspension, a five-year ban on new federal contracts for violators, and liability for unpaid wages plus equal liquidated damages, recovered amounts paid back to the workers [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal contractors and subcontractors currently paying below the living wage would bear higher labor costs, and to the extent those costs are passed on, federal agencies would pay more for contracted services. Contractors who violated the wage requirement would owe back wages, liquidated damages, and could lose federal business for five years [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Small business concerns and nonprofits whose CEO pay is no more than 25 times their lowest-paid worker's pay are entirely exempt, and apprentices and workers in training programs up to six months are excluded from the wage floor, narrowing who is protected [S2][S3].
Higher contract labor costs would flow into federal contracting budgets, meaning taxpayers could pay more for the same services on contracts affected by the wage floor [S3].
The wage requirement applies only to employees working on or hired in conjunction with a covered contract, leaving workers at the same company on non-federal work outside the floor [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is a genuine wage floor for workers paid out of federal dollars, with teeth: contract suspension, a five-year debarment, and double repayment of stolen wages. The costs fall on low-paying contractors and somewhat on federal procurement budgets. The exemptions for small businesses and six-month trainees are significant carve-outs that an honest supporter would acknowledge, and the reach is limited to contract-related work rather than all workers at covered firms.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, where it sat until the Congress ended — no committee vote, no floor vote, ever.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez introduced the bill on May 2, 2000, with 94 original cosponsors [S1][S4].
It was referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Government Reform Committee; no committee ever reported it [S1][S5].

In mid-2000 it was sent to the Government Management, Information and Technology subcommittee and the Workforce Protections subcommittee, and no further action followed before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors paying below the living wage are better off: they avoided a higher wage floor, debarment risk, and double-damages liability. The workers on their contracts never got the raise.

sides.party_line_note: All 94 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernard Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past referral [S4].

industries.note: The bill would force companies paid with federal dollars to raise wages to at least $8.20 an hour or the family-of-four poverty line, and to repay shortchanged workers double if caught. Keeping the bill from a vote preserved the freedom to pay contract workers poverty wages.
The bill exempts small business concerns from the living wage entirely, so this bill never applied to them; their contract labor costs stayed as they were.
Nonprofits were exempt unless their CEO earned more than 25 times their lowest-paid full-time employee, so high-pay nonprofits kept flexibility while modestly paying ones were spared a mandate.
